Question: What shocked you last week?
Old_Answer: The police came to my door. Asked me if it was true that I had the key to my neighbor’s house. I said I did. They then asked me if I would please open her door for them — they had been called by one of her friends and were alarmed by what she had said. So I did. The whole house was dark. All curtains were drawn. She was on the sofa, on the edge, it’s a large sofa shaped like the letter L. A blanket draped on her. Yes, she was breathing. Turned her head really slowly but wasn’t really seeing anything. She was drowsy. There were medicine wrappers on her lap and on the floor. She tried to kill herself. And she didn’t succeed, because she had called a former partner right before she took the pills. When I entered the room, followed by the police, she recognized me. And said my name. There was a strange tone in her voice. Almost one of betrayal. I’m conflicted, now. Did she want to die, and did she hate the fact that I interrupted her? Or did she send those dramatic text messages with the explicit desire for the police or someone else to come to her rescue? I’m still not sure. It could be an elaborate cry for attention. It could also be a genuine desire for help. It could be both suicidal ideation and desperation, both, at once. The morning she made her suicide attempt, she had been in my house. This same neighbor. Drunk, crying, at eight o’clock in the morning. Telling me she’ll never be a mother, a grandmother, that her life is “effectively over” and asking me what’s the point. She has given me the same exact talk before. Nothing about it made it feel different, this time around. But it was. Because she took an overdose that same day. An ambulance took her away and I haven’t seen her since.

Old_Answer: Here’s a photo from the 1990s of a man called Josef Fritzl, vacationing in Thailand without a care in the world. Fritzl was a businessman, married, father of seven, from Austria. He’d frequently travel the world. One year he’d be in Thailand. Another year he’d go to Africa. At times his friends would join him, they would drink, swim, lounge around resorts and float in the swimming pools of resorts… Fritzl was a doting grandfather of twenty. Three of his grandchildren lived with him and his wife — his youngest daughter Elizabeth, their mother, had ran away from home and joined a cult. So Fritzl and his wife raised their grandchildren. By all means, Josef had a charmed life. What no one knew? The three grandchildren he was raising were also his own biological children… their mother Elizabeth hadn’t joined a “cult”, she lived in a dungeon Fritzl had built inside his own basement. With three other children Fritzl also fathered there by his own daughter. Fritzl was arrested in 2008, at the age of 73. Because he had brought one of the “dungeon kids” to the hospital along with Elizabeth, his captive daughter, who then alerted authorities. Josef Fritzl remains in prison in Austria of this writing. He believes he should be freed, famously telling a judge: “I am just one man. But look inside the basements of other people… you would be surprised what you find!”

Old_Answer: If we strictly look at statistics for a moment and forget about fearmongering and sensationalism for just a minute… we find that there are several countries with a higher percentage of rapes and sexual assaults per percentage of population than India.[1] We find, for instance, that 27% of Chinese women who are married or in a relationship have experienced physical or sexual violence.[2] There’s this knee-jerk response in much of the world — they think of India, and they immediately think of a nation of perverts that defecate in the streets. It’s a grossly racist depiction, and it doesn’t hold up in terms of statistics. Because sure enough, Indian women are victimized on a daily basis. They are raped, assaulted, injured and have their honor besmirched by nasty creatures… but the same happens to women everywhere else, the world over. Even prosperous Sweden has a Sweden has 63.50 rape rate and around 5,960 incidents in per 100,000 citizens, to name another example… but Swedes aren’t stereotyped as a nation of rapists, last I checked. Nor are Chinese, or Jamaicans, or Americans. And yet in all these nations, sexual violence is rampant. Truth be told — India does not have a “special history” of women being targetted. Not anymore than other countries. India is both a huge country with 1.4 billion inhabitants, and a country that hasn’t outlawed protests. So when a high profile rape case happens in India, tens of thousands of angry women take to the streets. In China the same rape could happen but the protest would never take place or spread, because the state wouldn’t allow it. And in the West, all you’ll see is some performative celebrity outrage, but no tangible policy changes.

Old_Answer: One interesting connection I made was with a young Filipino man who was part of a cult. I wrote about our connection in another answer, years ago. He was faced with a devilish dilemma — either leave his fiancé of several years, or persuade her to join the cult for him. She didn’t want to, and he didn’t really want to make her do it. But if he didn’t, her eternal soul would be forfeit. And if he left, so would his. He wrestled with this moral dilemma for years as he remained loyal to the INC (Iglesia ni Cristo). He came to me for some advice on the matter. We talked. And talked. And talked. We talked for weeks. And finally he came to see my point of view — that true love means you would never force someone to switch faiths just to make things “easier” on you. He also came to realize, and accept for himself at long last, that the church he was part of was, indeed, a cult. Through our conversations he came to finally see and accept the absurdity of his faith. And decided to leave once and for all. His parents, sadly, were penalized for this and lost some standing in the community; that’s another way a cult can hold its wayward members emotionally hostage.
